title: Engines that make sub-100 °C heat worth converting

concept.text: The innovation would be a practical heat-to-electricity system that makes selected heat streams below 100 °C economically worth using. It would take heat from a source such as industrial coolant, convert part of that energy into electricity, and reject the remaining heat to a colder sink. Success would require useful electrical output after the system’s own pumps, cooling equipment, controls, and other auxiliaries consume their share.

The proposed advance is an integrated combination of conversion efficiency, power density, installed cost, and operating life. A low-temperature engine alone would not establish that capability: heat collection, heat exchangers, fluid circulation, electrical generation, and heat rejection must work together economically. This is an engineering and economic target within thermodynamic limits; the supplied record does not establish that it has been achieved.

significance.text: As conditional impact reasoning, an inexpensive and durable converter could make selected coolant and industrial waste-heat streams useful for electricity generation at sites where conversion currently does not pay. The direct consequence would be additional net electricity from an existing heat flow, provided that collecting the heat and maintaining a suitable cold sink do not consume the benefit. The supplied evidence does not identify or verify particular sites meeting those conditions.

A much larger contribution would depend on how much suitable heat is available, its temperature and operating schedule, the availability of colder sinks, installation constraints, maintenance costs, and the value of the electricity produced. As an application-level synthesis, electricity generation would also need to be compared with other useful destinations for the heat, including direct reuse. Converting heat into electricity is not automatically the most valuable use of every stream.

The revolutionary possibility is a change in the economics of an otherwise difficult energy resource. It would not make low-temperature heat equivalent to high-temperature fuel: a small temperature difference still limits the fraction convertible into work and leaves substantial heat to reject. A successful 1 kW prototype could establish a meaningful engineering result, but would not by itself establish broad economic viability, scalable deployment, or a large global energy contribution.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is economical, durable net electricity production from specified low-temperature sources and sinks. The thermodynamic constraint is central: for ideal reservoirs at 80 °C and 20 °C, the Carnot efficiency calculated using absolute temperatures is 1 − 293.15/353.15, approximately 17%. Half of that limit is approximately 8.5%. These are calculations for the proposed temperature pair, not measured engine performance; actual working-fluid temperatures and losses further constrain an implementation.

As engineering synthesis, limited conversion efficiency creates a difficult system tradeoff: useful electrical output requires processing a comparatively large heat flow, while transferring that heat through finite heat exchangers requires temperature differences that reduce the temperature span available to the engine. Increasing heat-exchanger area can improve thermal performance while adding material, installation cost, and size. Circulation and cooling must also use little enough power to preserve useful net output.

The concrete development barriers therefore include efficient conversion at the available temperature span; affordable heat collection and rejection; low pumping and other auxiliary losses; sufficient power per installed size and cost; and reliable operation under the chosen application's conditions. Materials, seals, surfaces, and working fluids would need to remain serviceable through that operating duty. These are proposed engineering requirements inferred from the concept, rather than a source-verified diagnosis of a particular existing machine.

Economic success also requires matching the converter to a real site. Source availability, heat-source cooling during extraction, sink warming, maintenance, and installation can change both output and return. The unresolved advance is their successful combination over a useful operating life, rather than maximizing one component’s efficiency in isolation. The supplied record does not establish which subsystem currently dominates the obstacle across different applications.

current_state.text: The supplied research states that low-temperature heat conversion is physically possible and has been demonstrated in various forms. It does not identify individual devices, demonstration dates, measured outputs, efficiencies, or endurance results. The review had no captured source text or artifacts with which to verify those demonstrations, so the record supports retaining the reported background with that limitation rather than describing a particular demonstrated system.

The research identifies Charles Geffroy, Drew Lilley, Pedro Sanchez Perez, and Ravi Prasher’s 2021 Joule paper, “Techno-economic analysis of waste-heat conversion,” DOI 10.1016/j.joule.2021.10.014. It attributes to that paper a modeled finding that conversion below 100 °C was uneconomic under the study’s assumptions, including an optimistic engine cost and a high capacity factor. This is a reported, model-dependent conclusion; it should not be read as a physical prohibition or as excluding every site and future design. No numerical engine-cost or capacity-factor assumptions are supplied.

The linked document is described in the research as an author manuscript, with the summary and model development identified as the relevant portions. However, the source index records no captured document or artifacts, and the review could not check the paper’s identity, completeness, modeled temperature range, assumptions, or conclusions against saved text. The research also reports that the publisher page returned HTTP 403. These access and capture limitations leave the attribution unverified in this record; they do not demonstrate that the attributed result is false.

The supplied review contains no bounded search results establishing subsequent developments through its stated assessment date of November 1, 2026. Consequently, this record cannot determine whether later systems have met the proposed capability, or whether the economic conclusion attributed to the 2021 model remains representative. Neither continued openness nor subsequent resolution is established by that absence.

completion_criteria.text: A proposed demanding demonstration is at least 1 kW of continuous net electrical output for 1,000 hours from a specified 80 °C source and 20 °C sink, at an efficiency of at least half the corresponding ideal-reservoir Carnot limit—approximately 8.5% for those temperatures. These are proposed evaluation thresholds, not established standards. Half-Carnot performance is not necessary for every economically viable application, and meeting it would not alone prove favorable economics.
completion_criteria.label: A proposed demanding demonstration is at least 1

completion_criteria.text: The proposed protocol should define net electrical efficiency as exported electrical energy after all necessary auxiliaries divided by thermal energy removed from the specified source, using a declared system boundary. It should identify where source and sink temperatures are measured, allowable temperature variation, whether operation is steady or changes over time, and how startup energy and external equipment are accounted for. Measurements should track source cooling or depletion, sink warming, heat-exchanger performance, and thermal and electrical energy balances.
completion_criteria.label: The proposed protocol should define net electrical efficiency

completion_criteria.text: Independent measurement should establish sustained output and efficiency with stated uncertainty, followed by reproducible operation on repeated runs or independently built units. The 1,000-hour run would demonstrate endurance over that interval; longer operation, degradation measurements, and maintenance evidence would be needed to support a claimed service life. Tests across additional temperatures, loads, and operating schedules would establish demonstrated breadth within those tested conditions, not universal applicability.
completion_criteria.label: Independent measurement should establish sustained output and efficiency

completion_criteria.text: A convincing application-level result should include full installed costs and a credible positive lifecycle return for a named use. The proposed analysis should disclose heat availability, electricity value, auxiliary consumption, maintenance, replacement assumptions, service life, and financing assumptions, and compare conversion with the relevant existing use or disposal of the heat. Sensitivity analysis should show which changes erase the return. This would establish an economic case within explicit practical boundaries, with broader deployment claims requiring additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: A convincing application-level result should include full installed

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MEC-01, “An engineering-predictive theory of turbulent flow,” could overlap through prediction of heat transfer and pressure losses in exchangers and fluid circuits. MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” and MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” could help predict losses and durability in moving machinery. Their targets are predictive capabilities; MEC-03 concerns economical net heat-to-electricity conversion in an integrated system.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-02, “Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts,” could reduce friction in implementations with relevant moving contacts. MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” and MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” could contribute to component durability or compactness. None of these capabilities alone resolves heat-exchanger cost, heat rejection, or the limited available work from a small temperature difference; MEC-03 also need not require them.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-05, “Programmable solids that become different load-bearing mechanisms,” and MEC-08, “Distributed actuators that simultaneously match skeletal muscle,” concern reconfiguration and actuation. They could intersect with particular converter mechanisms, but actuation performance and economical extraction of electricity from low-temperature heat are distinct objectives. MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” could aid design exploration without itself establishing thermal performance or lifecycle economics.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-06, “Macroscopic atomically precise mechanosynthesis,” MEC-09, “Mechanical self-replication of a production cell from feedstock,” and MEC-10, “Stress-directed growth of load-bearing structures,” concern fabrication, production autonomy, and structural formation. They might eventually affect how converters or components are manufactured, but those connections are conditional. MEC-03 does not require atomically precise fabrication, self-replication, or growing structures, and economical conversion would not demonstrate any of those capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-14, “Low-cost mechanical storage with high efficiency over long periods,” concerns retaining previously supplied energy for later use. MEC-03 concerns generating electricity from a heat flow and a colder sink. Storage could complement a converter when heat availability and electricity demand differ in time, but storage efficiency and heat-to-electricity efficiency describe different processes and require separate demonstrations.

change_log.reason: The useful target is the combination of net output, cost, durability, and thermal integration; the record does not establish its achievement.

change_log.change: Retained the reported 2021 economic finding while explicitly qualifying its attribution and model dependence.
change_log.reason: The research supplies a bibliographic reference and summary, but the review had no captured text to verify assumptions or conclusions. Missing evidence does not refute the result.

change_log.change: Added the approximately 17% Carnot limit and 8.5% half-Carnot benchmark for the proposed temperature pair.
change_log.reason: The review’s calculation makes the proposed efficiency target concrete while distinguishing an ideal-reservoir calculation from actual performance.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration with an efficiency denominator, system boundary, temperature tolerances, independent measurement, reproducibility, and lifecycle assumptions.
change_log.reason: These details address ambiguities identified in the review and make the proposed test interpretable without presenting it as an established standard.

change_log.reason: A finite prototype test cannot establish lifetime reliability, universal viability, or global impact.

unresolved_issues: The cited manuscript’s identity, completeness, modeled temperature range, engine-cost assumptions, capacity factor, and economic conclusions remain unverified against captured source text.
No specific low-temperature conversion demonstrations, with dates and measured performance, are documented in the supplied evidence.
The supplied record does not establish whether later developments met this capability or changed the relevance of the reported 2021 model.
A final demonstration protocol still needs exact system boundaries, temperature tolerances, measurement uncertainties, and operating conditions; the proposed definitions are not an adopted standard.
The named application, installed cost, maintenance requirements, full operating life, and lifecycle-return assumptions remain unspecified.
